items.question: what does this mean?
items.script:
say This is a matrix equation: a matrix times a vector equals another vector.
ring 620 250 150 | the matrix times the vector
say Think of it like a recipe: the numbers in the grid mix together to make the answer on the right.
say Here it's Ax = b, with A the grid, x the unknowns, and b the answer.
title Matrix equations, Ax = b

items.question: explain this like a story
items.script:
say Once upon a time, a teacher had a secret recipe: mix two numbers and get a special answer.
highlight 365 170 520 150 | the matrix, the vector, and the answer
say The grid of numbers is a machine. You feed it the unknown x and it spits out b.
say The lecturer is working out which x fits the answer, the way a detective finds the missing clue.
title Matrix equations as a story

items.question: show me step by step how to solve this
items.script:
say The board shows two equations, and I can read them as 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3.
highlight 380 170 400 150 | the two equations
say Step one: from the first equation, y = 2x.
say Step two: put that into the second: -x + 2(2x) = 3, so 3x = 3, which gives x = 1.
say Step three: then y = 2(1) = 2. Check: 2(1) - 2 = 0, and -1 + 4 = 3. Both work.
title Solving 2x2 system by substitution

items.question: how would they test this, exam style?
items.script:
say Exams often give a similar system and ask for one value, like x.
say Try it: what is x in 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3?
choices 1 | 2 | 3
say Hint: use y = 2x from the first equation, then substitute into the second.
title Exam practice: solving a 2x2 system

highlight 690 175 85 145 | look at this column
choices The vector [0, 3] | The grid of numbers | The unknown x

items.question: what is a matrix?
items.script:
say A matrix is a neat box of numbers, arranged in rows and columns.
highlight 420 175 240 130 | this grid is a matrix
say Think of a spreadsheet or a bingo card: numbers in rows and columns.
say Here the grid has 2 rows and 2 columns, so it's a 2 by 2 matrix.
title What is a matrix?

items.question: why do we write it as a matrix?
items.script:
say We write it as a matrix to keep the numbers tidy, like a shortcut for the whole system.
say Think of a long shopping list: a grid makes it quicker to read and work with.
say Instead of writing 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3 again and again, you write Ax = b once.
say The grid holds just the numbers, so computers and mathematicians can handle big systems easily.
title Why use matrices

items.question: what does the x mean here?
items.script:
say Here x is the unknown: the two numbers we are trying to find.
ring 395 232 32 | the unknown x
say Think of it like a locked box: the grid is the lock, and x is the code that opens it.
say In this system, x is the pair of values (x, y) that makes both equations true.
title What x means in Ax = b

items.question: what is a system of linear equations?
items.script:
say A system of linear equations is a group of equations that all share the same unknowns and must be true together.
highlight 420 175 240 130 | the two equations together
say Think of two friends who each give a clue: only one answer fits both clues at once.
say Here, 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3 form a system, and x = 1, y = 2 fits both.
title What is a system of linear equations?

items.question: can you visualize this?
items.script:
say Yes. Each equation is a straight line on a graph, and the answer is where the two lines cross.
say The first line is y = 2x, and the second is y = (x + 3) / 2.
say They cross at the point x = 1, y = 2, which is the one spot both equations share.
say Think of two paths on a map: the meeting point is the only place both paths reach together.
title Visualizing a 2x2 system as crossing lines

items.question: explain this diagram
items.script:
say This is a neural network reading a handwritten digit, here a 2.
ring 352 320 170 | the 784 input pixels
say Each dot is a neuron, and each column is a layer that passes its answer to the next.
ring 718 330 100 | the 10 outputs, digits 0 to 9
say The 784 dots are the pixels of the image, and the network picks the digit it thinks is most likely.
title Neural network reading digits

items.question: what are these circles?
items.script:
say These circles are neurons, tiny units that each hold one number.
ring 470 300 70 | one column of neurons
say Think of each neuron as a light bulb: brighter means a bigger number.
say Each neuron takes numbers from the layer before, mixes them, and passes one number on.
title What are neurons?

items.question: what do the lines between them mean?
items.script:
say Each line is a connection, and each one has a weight: a number that says how much it matters.
arrow 480 300 -> 580 300 | a line carries a weight
say Think of a volume knob: a big weight turns that signal up, a small one turns it down.
say The network learns by changing these weights until the digit guesses are right.
title Weights between neurons

items.question: how does a neural network learn?
items.script:
say It learns by guessing, checking how wrong it was, and nudging its weights a little.
say Think of practicing free throws: you miss, notice which way, and adjust your aim next time.
say It repeats this on thousands of example digits, so the weights slowly get better at spotting each one.
title How a neural network learns

items.question: explain this like a story
items.script:
say Once upon a time, a little robot looked at a messy handwritten 2 and had to guess what it was.
highlight 45 88 145 146 | the handwritten 2 it sees
say It passed the picture through its neurons, like a team of helpers each whispering one clue to the next.
say At the end, ten lights glowed, and the brightest one was its guess.
say Wrong guesses made it tweak its weights, so next time it looked a little wiser.
title Neural network as a story

items.question: what is the input layer?
items.script:
say The input layer is the first column of dots, the one that receives the image.
ring 352 320 45 | the input layer
say Each dot holds one pixel's brightness, and there are 784 of them, because the image is 28 by 28.
say Think of it like a row of doorbells: each one gets a single piece of the picture.
title The input layer

items.question: what is gradient descent?
items.script:
say Gradient descent is how the network slowly finds the best weights, step by step.
ring 1080 130 60 | the gradient descent video
say Think of walking down a foggy hill: you feel which way slopes down and take a small step that way.
say Each step lowers the error a bit, until the network reaches a low point where its guesses are good.
title Gradient descent

items.question: what is the output here?
items.script:
say The output is the last column, ten neurons labeled 0 to 9, one for each digit.
ring 708 335 115 | the output layer, digits 0 to 9
say The brightest neuron is the network's answer, like a quiz where the loudest buzzer wins.
say For this picture, the network should light up the 2 most.
title The output layer

items.question: show me visually how information flows
items.script:
say Information flows left to right, one layer at a time, like water through pipes.
arrow 360 320 -> 460 320 | pixels feed the hidden neurons
arrow 600 330 -> 695 330 | hidden neurons feed the outputs
say Each arrow means the numbers pass forward, getting mixed with the weights on the way.
title How information flows through layers

items.question: explain how video streaming works
items.script:
say Streaming means the video arrives in small pieces while you watch, instead of downloading the whole file first.
say Think of a water hose: the video flows to you in a steady stream, and your player catches each piece as it comes.
say The video is cut into tiny chunks at several quality levels. Your player picks the chunk quality that fits your internet speed, and switches if it slows down.
title How video streaming works

items.question: what is a variable in python?
items.script:
say A variable in Python is a name that holds a value, like a labeled box.
say Think of a box marked "score" that holds the number 10.
say You write it as score = 10, and then you can use score later in your code.
title Variables in Python

items.question: explain recursion
items.script:
say Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.
say Think of Russian nesting dolls: each doll holds a smaller doll, until you reach the tiniest one.
say Every recursive function needs a base case, a stop point, or it would keep calling itself forever.
title Recursion

items.question: what is an API?
items.script:
say An API is a set of rules that lets one program ask another program for something.
say Think of a restaurant menu: you pick a dish, the kitchen makes it, and you never enter the kitchen.
say The menu is the API: it lists what you can order and how to order it.
title What is an API?

items.question: what is compound interest?
items.script:
say Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, not just on your original money.
say Think of a snowball rolling down a hill: it picks up more snow as it grows, so it gets bigger faster.
say If you save 100 at 10% a year, you get 110, then 10% of 110 next year, which is 11.
title Compound interest

items.question: how do I solve 2x + 3 = 11?
items.script:
say Subtract 3 from both sides first: 2x = 8.
say Then divide both sides by 2: x = 4.
say Check it: 2 times 4 is 8, plus 3 is 11, so it works.
title Solving 2x + 3 = 11

items.question: what is the derivative of x squared?
items.script:
say The derivative of x squared is 2x.
say Think of it as the slope of the curve: at each point, how steeply x squared is rising.
say The rule: bring the power down in front, then subtract one from the power.
title Derivative of x squared
